title: Episode 59: The 1911 Inaugural Indianapolis 500: Ray Harroun and the Marmon Wasp

The 1911 Inaugural Indianapolis 500: Ray Harroun and the Marmon Wasp: How an intrepid engineer invented the rearview mirror and won the world's most famous race on 3.2 million paving bricks. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into this extraordinary chapter of the American story.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. On Memorial Day, May 30, 1911, eighty thousand roaring spectators gathered at the newly paved Indianapolis Motor Speedway to witness the birth of a motorsport legend. Forty thunderous, open-cockpit race cars took the green flag for the inaugural International Five-Hundred-Mile Sweepstakes. While every other car carried two men—a driver and a riding mechanic whose job was to watch for overtaking cars—a calm, thirty-two-year-old automotive engineer named Ray Harroun showed up alone in a sleek, yellow single-seat racer called the Marmon Wasp. To see who was coming up behind him, Harroun mounted a small piece of glass on his dashboard, inventing the automobile rearview mirror and driving straight into sporting immortality. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: CARL FISHER'S MUD AND STONE DREAM
In the first decade of the twentieth century, the American automobile industry was an explosive, chaotic frontier of dozens of independent manufacturers experimenting with steam, electricity, and internal combustion. But there was a critical technological bottleneck: America had virtually no paved roads suitable for testing high-speed automotive engineering. In nineteen oh-nine, an energetic, eccentric Indiana entrepreneur and bicycle racing champion named Carl G. Fisher gathered three fellow Indianapolis businessmen to solve the problem. Fisher purchased three hundred and twenty-eight acres of flat farmland five miles northwest of downtown Indianapolis and constructed a colossal two-and-a-half-mile rectangular oval racetrack with sweeping banked corners. Originally surfaced with crushed stone and two hundred and twenty thousand gallons of heavy road oil, the track hosted its first races in August nineteen oh-nine. The result was an unmitigated disaster: the flying stone surface disintegrated under the spinning wheels of heavy race cars, blinding drivers in dense dust clouds, causing catastrophic crashes, and claiming the lives of five people. Realizing the track must be completely rebuilt or abandoned, Fisher made a staggering financial gamble: he repaved the entire two-and-a-half-mile oval with three million two hundred thousand ten-pound culinary vitrified paving bricks, bonded with liquid cement. The legendary 'Brickyard' was born. The roar of racing engines echoed across the Indiana cornfields, signaling the rise of Indianapolis as the undisputed automotive manufacturing capital of the early twentieth century. Carl Fisher was a charismatic promoter with an iron will, having made millions through the manufacture of Prest-O-Lite acetylene automobile headlights before dedicating his fortune to testing and advancing automotive engineering on the open road.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GREAT FIVE-HUNDRED-MILE CHALLENGE
By late nineteen ten, Fisher and his management team realized that staging weekend series of short sprint races was failing to generate national enthusiasm or substantial ticket revenues. Fisher proposed a revolutionary concept: scrap the minor weekend events and stage a single, colossal annual spectacle—a grueling five-hundred-mile endurance race with an unprecedented prize purse of twenty-five thousand dollars in gold, equivalent to a fortune today. The five-hundred-mile distance was calculated to push human endurance and mechanical metallurgy to their absolute limits, requiring cars to race at sustained speeds over seventy miles an hour for nearly seven continuous hours. The event captured international attention. European racing dynasties entered champion cars: fiery Italian Fiats, roaring German Mercedes, and sleek French Peugeots, alongside American engineering marvels from Case, National, Lozier, Simplex, and Marmon. On the morning of May thirtieth, nineteen eleven, special passenger trains from Chicago, New York, and St. Louis disgorged over eighty thousand spectators, packing the wooden grandstands in the largest sporting gathering in American history. Specially chartered Pullman trains lined the sidings, disgorging wealthy industrialists, European dignitaries, and working-class racing fans eager to witness the ultimate test of man and machine. Early settlers faced immense hardships carving farms and homesteads from the dense eastern woodlands, battling disease, inclement weather, and frontier isolation with unyielding resolve. European road racers and American dirt-track drivers alike warned that running five hundred continuous miles on a surface composed of sharp paving bricks would destroy tires and shatter suspensions, predicting that fewer than ten cars would finish the punishing contest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: ENTER THE MARMON WASP AND THE FLYING SINGLE-SEATER
Among the forty qualified entries was the Marmon Motor Car Company, an elite, high-precision engineering firm based in Indianapolis. Marmon's chief engineer and test driver was thirty-two-year-old Ray Harroun. Born in Pennsylvania, Harroun was a mild-mannered, intellectual bachelor with a degree in engineering who had won the national driving championship in nineteen ten. Harroun had formally announced his retirement from racing to focus on designing production road cars, but Howard Marmon coaxed him back for one final competition. Harroun designed the race car himself: the Marmon Model 32, nicknamed the 'Wasp' because of its bright yellow paint, sharp black pinstripes, and an aerodynamic tapered tail that terminated in a long, horizontal stabilization fin. But Harroun's car caused an immediate, explosive controversy in the garage area. Every other car on the starting grid was a two-seater carrying a driver and a 'riding mechanic.' In nineteen eleven, riding mechanics were indispensable: they manually pumped oil pressure with a hand pump, monitored fuel gauges, tightened loose engine bolts with wrenches at high speed, and constantly peered over their shoulders to warn the driver of cars attempting to pass. Harroun's Marmon Wasp was a narrow, lightweight single-seater with room for only the driver. The Marmon Wasp was built with aircraft-grade aluminum and hand-forged steel alloy, featuring a six-cylinder four-hundred-and-seventy-seven-cubic-inch engine that purred with Swiss-watch precision. The spirit of American innovation was evident in every workshop and meeting hall, where practical mechanics and visionary thinkers sought solutions to the most challenging obstacles of their era. Marmon Chief Engineer Howard Marmon chose a six-cylinder T-head engine that produced a modest eighty-five horsepower, prioritizing mechanical reliability, balanced weight distribution, and reduced tire wear over raw brute top speed.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE INVENTION OF THE REARVIEW MIRROR
Rival drivers erupted in fury, petitioning Speedway officials to disqualify the Marmon Wasp on safety grounds. They argued that a lone driver without a riding mechanic would be unable to see overtaking vehicles and would cause fatal pileups on the crowded brick oval. Harroun remained unperturbed. Remembering a horse-drawn carriage driver he had seen in Chicago in nineteen oh-four who had a small mirror mounted to his dashboard to watch traffic, Harroun went to a local hardware shop. He purchased a three-by-eight-inch rectangular glass mirror, mounted it inside a steel bracket, and fastened it to four metal struts perched directly above the center of his dashboard, angled so he could see the track behind him without turning his head. Speedway judges inspected the contraption, recognized that Harroun had an unobstructed view of approaching traffic, and allowed the Marmon Wasp to start. It was the very first recorded use of a rearview mirror on an automobile in human history—an innovation that would within a decade become standard safety equipment on every passenger vehicle manufactured across the globe. Mechanics in the pits scoffed at the small glass mirror, betting that engine vibrations would shatter the lens within five laps of high-speed racing on the jarring bricks. News of these extraordinary events traveled by telegraph and steam train across the nation, captivating readers in major eastern cities and inspiring future generations of pioneers and inventors. Rival drivers initially protested Harroun's solo entry, demanding that the American Automobile Association require every entrant to carry a riding mechanic to warn of approaching vehicles, until Harroun unveiled his innovative mounted mirror.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ROAR OF THE FORTY
At ten o'clock on Memorial Day morning, Carl Fisher led the field in a Stoddard-Dayton touring car for the world's first rolling pace lap, pulling off the track as starter Fred Wagner unfurled the red flag. Forty unmuffled racing engines roared simultaneously, shaking the grandstands with a concussive shockwave of noise and choking blue castor oil smoke. The inaugural race was an epic trial of mechanical attrition. The rough vitrified bricks acted like abrasive grinding wheels against the primitive, natural rubber pneumatic tires of the era. Tire blowouts occurred every few laps, sending cars spinning into the wooden inner guardrails and scattering splinters of ash and oak across the track. While rival drivers pushed their engines to their absolute mechanical limits, speeding at eighty miles an hour and blowing out tires every twenty laps, Ray Harroun drove with calculated mathematical discipline. He paced the Marmon Wasp at an even, controlled average speed of seventy-five miles per hour, conserving his engine bearings and babying his Firestone tires so effectively that he made only four pit stops during the entire five-hundred-mile marathon. Harroun maintained a rhythmic, steady cadence lap after lap, smoothly guiding the yellow racer through the treacherous oil-slicked turns while competitors pushed too hard and crashed. The enduring lessons of this historic chapter continue to resonate across American culture, reminding us of the courage, sacrifice, and vision of those who shaped the destiny of our nation. Pneumatic tires of the era were notoriously fragile, shedding treads under the intense friction of the hot paving bricks and forcing pit crews to perform exhausting tire changes using heavy iron spoons and manual air pumps.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE FINAL LAP AND THE SCORING CONTROVERSY
As the race entered its final fifty miles, only a dozen battered cars remained running. Harroun took the lead, battling wheel-to-wheel against Ralph Mulford in a massive white Lozier and David Bruce-Brown in a monstrous nine-hundred-cubic-inch Fiat. In the chaotic, manual scoring stand, where judges tracked cars using paper score sheets and spinning number wheels, a multi-car crash on the front stretch caused temporary confusion among the scorers. Mulford pitted for a tire change, and Harroun surged ahead on the bricks. At four twenty-three in the afternoon, after six hours, forty-two minutes, and eight seconds of grueling competition, Ray Harroun guided the yellow Marmon Wasp across the chalk line, greeted by the waving green checkered flag. His average speed for the five hundred miles was seventy-four point six miles per hour. Mulford and the Lozier team initially contested the finish, claiming they had made up a lap during the scoring confusion, but after an exhaustive overnight audit of the official timing tape, Speedway judges confirmed Ray Harroun as the rightful and undisputed winner of the inaugural Indianapolis 500. The scoring wire hummed with telegraph clicks as officials audited the split times, confirming that Harroun meticulous strategy had earned him the premier crown of global motorsport. The roaring crowd in the wooden grandstands cheered deliriously as the yellow Marmon Wasp crossed the finish line after six hours and forty-two minutes of relentless racing, having averaged seventy-four point six miles per hour over the distance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF THE BRICKYARD
True to his word, Ray Harroun collected his ten-thousand-dollar winner's check, stepped out of the Marmon Wasp, and never drove in another competitive automobile race, retiring permanently to pursue a brilliant career as an automotive inventor, holding over twenty industrial patents for carburetors and braking systems. The Marmon Wasp, preserved in its original racing condition with its iconic dashboard mirror and yellow tail fin, remains the crown jewel of the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum. The inaugural 1911 race established the Indianapolis 500 as 'The Greatest Spectacle in Racing'—a crucible of technological innovation that gave the world not only the rearview mirror, but balloon tires, aerodynamic streamlining, seat belts, and modern automotive safety engineering, proving that the courage of pioneer drivers on three million paving bricks helped build the modern world on wheels. Modern race cars traveling at two hundred and thirty miles an hour still race across the historic yard of bricks at the start-finish line, honoring the pioneer drivers of nineteen eleven. The inaugural 500 established the Indianapolis Motor Speedway as the undisputed capital of world auto racing, accelerating the development of four-wheel brakes, streamlined aerodynamics, and advanced engine alloys throughout the twentieth century.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Ray Harroun and the Marmon Wasp proved that cool intellect, careful preparation, and simple innovation can outrace raw horsepower. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey east into Ohio to uncover the forgotten swamp that shaped a state: the Great Black Swamp.
